text: On 23 November 2022, dairy worker Janak Patel was murdered during a robbery at the Rose Cottage Superette in Sandringham, Auckland, New Zealand. The incident occurred at 8pm when Patel, a recent Indian migrant who had moved to Auckland from Hamilton just days before, and his wife were in a backroom living area of the store when masked offender Frederick Gilbert Hobson, an Ōtāhuhu resident repatriated from Australia, entered armed with a knife. Hobson had been stalking the area for 45 minutes, hiding in a telephone booth, and after confronting Patel, used a knife to attack him, stabbing him six times, including in the chest and back. Patel managed to fight back with a hockey stick, wrestled with Hobson, and was forced to the ground before being stabbed in the neck. Hobson fled with the stolen cash register, which was later found in a rubbish bin, and the suspect was confronted by Patel, who provided a description to police. On 24 November, police released images of the suspect, described as wearing a black cap, black and white bandanna, dark top, and black trousers emblazoned with "Raiders," and launched a homicide investigation, confirming they were hunting for a lone man. By 25 November, police had identified two suspects from CCTV footage showing two men and a black car, later confirmed as a dark-coloured Honda Inspire, and arrested them; a 34-year-old man was charged with murder and aggravated robbery, and a 42-year-old man with robbery. On 27 November, a 36-year-old man was charged with robbery. The three defendants appeared in the Auckland High Court on 14 December 2022, where the 34-year-old man (interim name suppression) and 42-year-old Shane Tane pleaded not guilty to robbery and murder charges, while Henry Ford, the third defendant, was granted a stay of proceedings due to terminal illness. On 8 March 2023, Fred and Tane had their charges upgraded from aggravated robbery to murder, and Hobson's name suppression lapsed. On 13 March 2024, Frederick Hobson pleaded guilty to murder and aggravated robbery. On 26 June 2024, Hobson was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum non-parole period of 15 years, and Shane Tane was sentenced to four years and six months for aggravated robbery. Henry Ford remained in stay of proceedings. Hobson's lawyer stated he was ashamed and remorseful, citing homelessness, unemployment, and drug addiction as contributing factors. Victim impact statements were heard during sentencing. In response to the incident, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern faced criticism from ACT Party leader David Seymour for not visiting Sandringham or postponing her trip to the Chatham Islands, which she defended by stating she had consulted community leaders and did not want to interfere with the investigation. On 26 November, Ardern met with Patel’s family and community leaders, acknowledged police efforts, and confirmed the government was investigating ways to support small businesses with security measures. On 28 November, the government announced a new retail crime package including a fog cannon subsidy scheme, a NZ$4 million fund for local councils in Auckland, Hamilton, and the Bay of Plenty, and expanded eligibility of the existing NZ$6 million Retail Crime Prevention Fund to include aggravated robberies. Dairy and Business Owners Association chairperson Sunny Kaushal announced a nationwide protest following Patel’s funeral, with thousands of dairies and small businesses ceasing operations for at least two hours, and called for self-defence laws to allow owners to use "acceptable force." Sandringham Business Association chair Jithin Chittibomma criticized the government for ignoring retail concerns. On 26 November, the Migrant Workers Association held a candlelit vigil outside the store, and on 28 November, the Dairy and Business Owners Group staged a nationwide protest, including a vigil outside Ardern’s electorate office in Mt Albert and others across the country. By 3 December, a Givealittle page had raised NZ$91,000 for Patel’s family, and by 23 December, over NZ$100,000 had been raised. In March 2022, Stuff reported a surge in retail crime including "ram raids," shoplifting, and repeat offending, prompting businesses to deploy countermeasures such as stab-proof vests, radios, body cameras, automatic number plate recognition, and facial recognition systems. In response, the New Zealand Police created a national retail investigation unit, which by October 2022 had dealt with over 70 offenders and laid nearly 600 charges. A University of Otago study estimated retail theft cost retailers NZ$1 billion annually and that retailers spent NZ$500 million a year on security, with retail crime costing the average household NZ$800 per year. Retail NZ chief executive Greg Harford estimated retail crime cost the average household NZ$800 annually. According to Kaushal, dairy and convenience store theft increased by 30 percent (1,402 offences) in the first 11 months of 2021 compared to 2020, while arrests for such crimes declined by 23 percent. The New Zealand Herald reported that retail crime incidents, including shoplifting and "ram raids," had doubled from 4,000 to under 8,000 between 2017 and the first six months of 2022, citing Police data. A 2019 Retail NZ survey estimated that 70% of retail crime was unreported. Police attributed the increase to improved reporting, while the National Party blamed it on Labour’s "soft on crime" policies. By late August 2022, police secured NZ$6 million in government funding for the Small Retailer Crime Prevention Fund to help small businesses install countermeasures such as shatterproof glass, bollards, fog cannons, and roller doors. Companies also hired door staff to deter offenders. In December 2014, Australia amended its Migration Act 1958 to make it easier to deport non-citizens imprisoned for at least one year. By March 2022, 2,544 New Zealanders had been deported from Australia over seven years, contributing to a surge in crime including over 2,000 dishonesty convictions, 1,387 violent crime convictions, 861 drug and anti-social behavior offenses, and 57 sexual crime offenses. Several Australian-based bikie gangs, including the Comanchero and Mongols, expanded into New Zealand. Police Commissioner Andrew Coster and National Party leader Christopher Luxon attributed the rising crime and gang membership to the repatriation of New Zealand deportees from Australia.
